title: Monotonic stack
sub: Daily Temperatures and Largest Rectangle in Histogram: the nearest greater and smaller in O(n)
cards/0/title: The problem and the “next greater” signal
cards/0/body:
Daily Temperatures (LeetCode #739). Given daily temperatures t, 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁵, 30 ≤ t[i] ≤ 100. For each day, answer how many days you have to wait for a strictly warmer one; if there is none, 0.

This is the next greater element problem: for each element find the nearest one to the right that is larger. Signals in the statement: “the nearest greater or smaller to the left or right”, “how long to wait”, “how far does it extend”, “who blocks it first”. Related problems: Next Greater Element (#496, #503), Online Stock Span (#901) and Largest Rectangle in Histogram (#84) — the second problem of this lesson.

In a game: in a 2D terrain profile (the column heights of a tile map), for each column find the first one to its right that is taller: that is where a horizontal ray cast from its top will hit.
cards/0/code:
int[] ans = DailyTemperatures(new[] { 73, 74, 75, 71, 69, 72, 76, 73 });
// [1, 1, 4, 2, 1, 1, 0, 0]: after 75° you wait 4 days — until 76°
cards/1/q: Where does the “nearest greater or smaller” technique apply? Select all.
cards/1/options/0: For each day — how many consecutive days, including this one, the stock price was not above today’s
cards/1/options/1: For each tower on a line — the nearest taller tower to its right
cards/1/options/2: For each histogram bar — how far left and right it extends before meeting a lower one
cards/1/options/3: The sum of every k consecutive numbers
cards/1/options/4: A pair of numbers adding up to target in a sorted array
cards/1/explain: The stock price is Online Stock Span (#901): the nearest earlier day with a higher price, and the distance to it is the answer. The tower is the next greater to the right in its purest form. The bar needs the nearest smaller on both sides — that is the histogram from the second half of the lesson. The sum of k in a row is a sliding window, the pair with a sum is converging pointers: neither asks about the nearest neighbour by value.
cards/2/title: The naive solution and its cost
cards/2/body:
For each day i walk right until you find a warmer day. If the warmer day is close, that is quick. But if there is none, the scan runs to the end of the array.

The worst case is many days that never get a warmer one: all temperatures equal or decreasing. Then each day scans the whole tail: n(n − 1)/2 comparisons, O(n²). For n = 10⁵ that is about 5·10⁹ — tens of seconds against a one-second limit.

Note that the narrow temperature range (30–100) does not save you here. It bounds the values, not the distance to the answer.
cards/3/q: n = 10⁵. On which input does the naive scan run longest?
cards/3/options/0: Every day has the same temperature, say 50°
cards/3/options/1: The temperature strictly rises every day
cards/3/explain: With equal temperatures nobody has a strictly warmer day, so every day scans the whole tail: about 5·10⁹ comparisons. With rising temperatures each day finds its answer on the very next day — O(n). With random temperatures a warmer day is usually close; only the hottest days search for long.
cards/3/wrong/1: When temperatures rise, the answer is always the next day: the inner loop makes one comparison and exits. That is O(n).
cards/3/wrong/2: With random values a warmer day is usually a few steps away. Only the days that nothing beats scan the whole tail, and there are few of them.
cards/4/title: The idea: a stack of those still waiting
cards/4/body:
What work does the scan repeat? It walks past the same days again and again. Look at the days that, by the time we reach i, are still waiting for a warmer one: their temperatures do not increase from left to right. If an earlier day were colder than a later one, the later day would already be its answer.

Keep these days in a stack of indices. Day i arrives: while the top is colder than t[i], the top has its answer — Pop and ans[j] = i − j. Then push i: now it waits too. Why look only at the top: it is the latest and the coldest of those waiting. If i is not warmer than the top, it is not warmer than anyone deeper either.

Invariant: the stack holds the indices of days without an answer, and their temperatures do not increase from bottom to top. Hence the name — a monotonic stack.

Why O(n) despite the inner while. Each index is pushed once and popped at most once: at most 2n stack operations in total, however long the while spins on a single step. Time is O(n) amortized, memory O(n). Store indices, not temperatures: t[j] gives the temperature, and the distance has to be computed from the index.
cards/4/flow/1: while t[top] < t[i]: j = Pop(), ans[j] = i − j
cards/4/flow/3: at the end the stack holds days with no answer: ans = 0
cards/5/explain: Pop while the top is strictly colder: the statement says “strictly warmer”. With <= a day of the same temperature would close a waiting one, and on [70, 70, 75] the first day’s answer would become 1 instead of 2. The wait is i − j days: j comes before i. Push the index, not the temperature — otherwise you cannot compute the distance or know which cell of ans to write.
cards/6/task: Step through [73, 74, 75, 71, 69, 72, 76, 73]. The rig stops twice when 72° arrives and asks what the code does to the stack.
cards/6/goal/asks/0/q: Day 5, 72°. The stack holds days 2 (75°), 3 (71°), 4 (69°), with 4 on top. What does the code do?
cards/6/goal/asks/0/explain: The code compares with the top only: 69° < 72°, so day 4 got warmer after 5 − 4 = 1 day. It moves further down the stack on the next iteration of the while.
cards/6/goal/asks/1/options/1/label: push 5: one day has been handled already
cards/6/goal/asks/1/q: ans[4] is written. The top is now day 3 (71°). What next?
cards/6/goal/asks/1/explain: The while keeps going: 71° < 72°, ans[3] = 5 − 3 = 2. The next top is day 2 (75°), which is warmer, so the while stops and 5 goes on top. One warm day closed two waiting ones: those pops are paid for by their earlier pushes — that is where O(n) comes from.
cards/7/title: Largest Rectangle: the nearest smaller on both sides
cards/7/body:
Largest Rectangle in Histogram (LeetCode #84, hard). Bars of width 1 with heights h, 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁵, 0 ≤ h[i] ≤ 10⁴. Find the area of the largest rectangle that lies entirely inside the histogram. On [2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3] the answer is 10: height 5 over bars 2 and 3.

Naively: from each bar expand left and right while the neighbours are not lower — O(n²), up to 10¹⁰ steps on equal heights.

The idea. The height of the best rectangle equals the height of some bar j — otherwise it could be raised. A rectangle of height h[j] extends from the nearest lower bar on the left to the nearest lower bar on the right. A stack of indices with increasing heights gives both boundaries at once. When bar i arrives and is not taller than the top, it is the top’s right boundary. Pop the top; the new top is the nearest lower bar on the left, so the left boundary is left = top + 1, and if the stack is empty, left = 0 — the popped bar was the lowest since the start. The width is i − left.

The sentinel. The loop runs up to i == n with height 0: it is lower than everything and pops whatever is left. Without it, rectangles that nothing blocked on the right are never counted.

Equal heights. The >= condition also pops an equal bar too early — its width comes out short. That is not a bug: the last of the equal bars counts the rectangle of that height in full. Each index enters and leaves once: O(n) time, O(n) memory. The answer is at most 10⁵ · 10⁴ = 10⁹ — it fits in an int.
cards/8/q: The code popped bar j, and the stack is now empty. What width does it use for the rectangle of height h[j] at step i?
cards/8/options/0: i: there is nothing lower to the left, the rectangle extends from index 0
cards/8/options/2: i − j: from the popped bar to the current one
cards/8/explain: An empty stack means there is no bar lower than h[j] to the left of j: everything to the left that was taller has already been popped. The rectangle of height h[j] starts at index 0 and ends before i — width i. For example, on [6, 5, 2] at i = 2 we pop the 5: width 2, area 10.
cards/8/wrong/1: Width 1 happens only when the nearest lower bar on the left is right next to it. An empty stack says there is no lower bar on the left at all.
cards/8/wrong/2: There may be taller bars left of j that were popped earlier: the rectangle extends over them too. On [6, 5, 2] the five has i − j = 1, while the correct width is 2.
cards/9/task: Step through [2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3]. The rig stops twice and asks which rectangle the code counts: look for the left boundary in the stack.
cards/9/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: push 4: two is taller than one
cards/9/goal/asks/0/q: i = 4, height 2. The six has already been popped. The stack holds indices 1 (height 1) and 2 (height 5), with 2 on top. What next?
cards/9/goal/asks/0/explain: 5 ≥ 2 — pop it. The new top is index 1, so left = 2 and the width is 4 − 2 = 2: the five extends over indices 2 and 3. The six is taller and was popped earlier, but a rectangle of height 5 passes over it too. Area 10 is a new record.
cards/9/goal/asks/1/q: End of the array: i = 6, a sentinel of height 0. The three has been popped. The stack holds indices 1 (height 1) and 4 (height 2). Which rectangle does the code count for the two?
cards/9/goal/asks/1/explain: Below the two is index 1, so left = 2 and the width is 6 − 2 = 4: bars 2–5 are all at least 2 tall. Area 8 is less than 10, the record stands. Without the sentinel this rectangle would never be counted: nothing to the right pushed the two out.
cards/10/q: On [2, 1, 2] this code returns 4 instead of 3. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/10/explain: The top below the popped bar is the nearest lower bar, and it is not part of the rectangle: the left boundary is top + 1. Here the width is one too large. At the sentinel i = 3 we pop the last two (index 2), and below it is index 1 of height 1: the code takes width 3 − 1 = 2 and area 4, although a height of 2 does not fit over the one.
cards/11/title: The link to rain water, and variations
cards/11/body:
Trapping Rain Water (solution 3 in the two-pointer unit) is the same skeleton mirrored: a stack of non-increasing heights, popped by a taller bar. The popped bar is the bottom of a puddle, the new top is the left wall, i is the right wall. The common scheme behind all these problems: a popped element learns both boundaries at once — the right one (who popped it) and the left one (who is below it in the stack).

Which stack to use. Looking for the nearest greater — the stack decreases and a greater element pops it. Looking for the nearest smaller — the stack increases and a smaller element pops it. The popped element gets its answer “to the right”; the element being pushed gets its answer “to the left”: the top after the pops.

A circular array (Next Greater Element II, #503): the first element follows the last. Walk indices 0…2n − 1 and take nums[i % n]; push only when i < n.

Maximal Rectangle (#85): a matrix of 0s and 1s, the largest rectangle of ones. For each row, heights[c] is how many ones in a row go up from it; every row becomes a histogram. Time O(rows · cols). In a game: the largest free rectangular plot for a building on a tile map is exactly this problem; a 256 × 256 map is 65,536 cells in one pass.
cards/11/deep:
Amortization, formally. Take the stack size as the potential. Step i does k pops and one push: the actual cost is k + 1, the potential changes by 1 − k, the amortized cost is 2. Summed over all steps that is at most 2n plus the initial potential of 0. It is the same argument as for List<T>.Add with doubling, except the “expensive” steps are paid for not by earlier cheap inserts but by the fact that each element can be popped only once.

Two passes instead of one. You can compute prevLess[i] and nextLess[i] separately (two monotonic passes, left to right and right to left) and then take max(h[i] · (nextLess[i] − prevLess[i] − 1)). Also O(n), more memory, but each boundary is easy to check on its own. With equal heights one pass uses a strict comparison and the other a non-strict one — otherwise counting problems (Sum of Subarray Minimums, #907) count equal ranges twice.

Without allocations. new Stack<int>() on every call is an object and an array for the garbage collector; in LargestFreeArea above that is one allocation per row. Keep the stack in a field and call Clear(), or simpler, use an int[] st of length n + 1 and a top index. Such code moves unchanged into a Burst job over a NativeArray<int>: for a map that changes every frame, that is a fitting answer to “what about 1024 × 1024?”.
cards/12/q: You are solving Largest Rectangle in Histogram out loud. Put the steps in order.
cards/12/items/0: Clarify: bars have width 1, heights ≥ 0, n up to 10⁵, the answer up to 10⁹ — fits in an int
cards/12/items/1: Name the naive approach: expand sideways from each bar — O(n²)
cards/12/items/2: Idea: the best rectangle’s height is some bar’s height, so you need the nearest smaller on the left and the right
cards/12/items/3: A stack of indices with increasing heights: a popped bar learns its right boundary i and its left one — the new top
cards/12/items/4: Write the code with a sentinel of height 0 at the end
cards/12/items/6: Complexity O(n), memory O(n); edge cases: all heights equal, heights strictly increasing
cards/12/explain: The problem and the cost of the naive approach, then the observation about height and boundaries, from it the stack and the code, a run on the example, and the complexity at the end. Strictly increasing heights test the sentinel: without it nothing gets popped.
